accepted.question_text: Does every subgroup H of an infinite-dimensional Lie group G admit a smooth manifold structure making H an initial Lie subgroup of G? Here this means that, for every k in N union {infinity}, H is C^k-initial in G in the sense that the inclusion map lambda: H -> G is C^k and every map f: X -> H from a C^k-manifold X is C^k whenever lambda o f is C^k, and moreover the induced tangent map L(lambda): L(H) -> L(G) is injective.

evidence.quote: We describe a subgroup of an infinite-dimensional Lie group which is not an initial Lie subgroup (Section 1). This answers [21, Problem II.6], the "Initial Subgroup Problem," in the negative.

Following [21, Definition II.6.1], we say that a subgroup H ⊆ G is an initial Lie subgroup if it can be given a smooth manifold structure which makes H a Lie group, is Ck-initial in G for each k ∈ N ∪ {∞}, and gives rise to an injective tangent map L(λ) := T1(λ): L(H) → L(G).
Theorem 1.3 For each k ∈ N ∪ {∞}, the additive subgroup N := ℓ∞ of bounded sequences is not a Ck-initial submanifold of M := RN. In particular, it is not an initial Lie subgroup.

accepted.question_text: If G = lim-> Gn is the direct limit of an ascending sequence G1 subseteq G2 subseteq ... of finite-dimensional real Lie groups with smooth inclusion homomorphisms, must every subgroup H of G be an initial Lie subgroup of G? Equivalently, can H be equipped with the direct-limit Lie group structure coming from Hn := Gn intersection H so that the inclusion H -> G is strongly C^k-initial for every k in N union {infinity}?
accepted.context_brief: Subgroups of direct limit Lie groups

evidence.quote: We show that every subgroup of a direct limit G = lim−→ Gn of finite-dimensional Lie groups is an initial Lie subgroup (Section 2). This answers [21, Problem VII.3] in the affirmative.

Theorem 2.1 Let G1 ⊆ G2 ⊆ · · · be finite-dimensional Lie groups, such that the inclusion map Gn → Gn+1 is a smooth homomorphism for each n ∈ N. Let G = lim−→ Gn be the direct limit Lie group, and H ⊆ G be a subgroup. Equip Hn := Gn ∩ H with the finite-dimensional real Lie group structure induced by Gn and H with the Lie group structure making it the direct limit Lie group H = lim−→ Hn. Then the manifold structure on H is strongly Ck-initial in G, for all k ∈ N ∪ {∞}. Thus H is an initial Lie subgroup of G.

accepted.question_text: If G = lim-> Gn is the direct limit of an ascending sequence of finite-dimensional Lie groups with smooth inclusion homomorphisms, is G a topological group with Lie algebra in the sense of Hofmann and Morris? That is, do the continuous one-parameter subgroups Hom_c(R, G) carry the vector-space and Lie-bracket operations specified by Definition 3.1, with addition given by the Trotter-type limit of (gamma(t/n) eta(t/n))^n and bracket given by the commutator limit, so that Hom_c(R, G) becomes a topological Lie algebra naturally identified with L(G)?
accepted.context_brief: Direct limits as topological groups with Lie algebra

evidence.quote: We show that every direct limit G = lim−→ Gn of finite-dimensional Lie groups is a topological group with Lie algebra in the sense of [16] (Section 3). This answers [21, Problem VII.2] in the affirmative.

Definition 3.1 G is called a topological group with Lie algebra if (a) (γ + η)(t) := limn→∞(γ(t/n)η(t/n))n exists for all γ, η ∈ Homc(R, G), and maps γ + η : R → G so obtained are continuous homomorphisms; (b) Homc(R, G) is a topological vector space with the addition defined in (a) and the scalar multiplication (8); and (c) There exists a continuous bilinear map [., .]: Homc(R, G) × Homc(R, G) → Homc(R, G) making it a Lie algebra.
Theorem 3.4 For each direct limit Lie group G = lim−→ Gn as in 3.3, the mapping ΓG : L(G) → Homc(R, G) is a homeomorphism and thus G is a topological group with Lie algebra.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a sigma-compact finite-dimensional smooth manifold of dimension n > 0, let p be a point of M, and let Diff_c(M)_{p,0} be the subgroup of compactly supported smooth diffeomorphisms fixing p whose tangent map at p has positive determinant. Is every formal diffeomorphism of R^n whose linear part has positive determinant realized as the Taylor series at p of some element of Diff_c(M)_{p,0}? Equivalently, is the Taylor-series homomorphism T_p^infinity: Diff_c(M)_{p,0} -> G^n_f(R)_0 surjective?

evidence.quote: Moreover, we prove a result by the author announced in [21], which answers a question posed in an earlier, unpublished version of the survey.

Borel's Theorem for Diffeomorphisms. Let a finite-dimensional smooth manifold M of dimension n be given, p ∈ M and φ be a local chart around p such that φ(p) = 0. For each γ ∈ Diffc(M), let T∞_p(γ) denote the Taylor series of φ ◦ γ ◦ φ−1 around 0. Then T∞_p : Diffc(M)p,0 → Gfn(R)0 is a surjective homomorphism of Lie groups.
In this case, the surjectivity of T∞_p : Diffc(Rn)p,0 → Gfn(R)0 has been established in Lemma 4.2. The Chain Rule for Taylor Polynomials entails that T∞_p is a homomorphism of groups.

evidence.quote: In [3], it is shown that the group Ghn(C) of germs of analytic diffeomorphisms around 0 ∈ Cn (as first considered in [22]) is a regular Lie group in Milnor's sense. This answers the first half of [21, Problem VI.5] in the affirmative.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Using a Frobenius theorem for co-Banach distributions, one obtains an existence result for integral subgroups, and hence [21, Problem VI.4] has an affirmative answer.

evidence.quote: Using a version of the Frobenius Theorem for co-Banach distributions on infinite-dimensional manifolds, one obtains the following result concerning integral subgroups in the sense of [21, Definition IV.4.7]. Let G be a Lie group modelled on a locally convex space and h ⊆ L(G) be a Lie subalgebra such that L(G) = h ⊕ X for some Banach space X ⊆ L(G). Then there exists an integral subgroup H ⊆ G such that L(H) = h. Note that a complement X always exists if h has finite codimension. Hence [21, Problem VI.4] has an affirmative answer.
